word_order: SVO | Sentences show a canonical Subject–Verb–Object order (e.g. 'Apple CEO Steve Jobs unveiled the device' — S V O).
register: edited, written expository prose (news/encyclopedic/technical style; formally edited factual sentences).
clause_boundary_signals: complementizer clauses (that — introduces embedded clauses and complements)
relative pronouns/clauses (who, which — introduce relative clauses attached to noun phrases)
subordinating conjunctions introducing dependent clauses (although, because)
non_boundary_traps: initial adverbial/prepositional phrases (for over a thousand years, around 60 cases — often sentence-initial but attach to a matrix clause)
appositives and parentheticals set off inside clauses (live on television; Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Group — interrupt the main clause without ending it)
noun-internal genitives/possessives (Auckland's National Women's Hospital — possessive morphology inside a single NP, not a clause break)
unstable_prefix_signals: introductory subordinators and prepositional phrases (Because, While — after these tokens the eventual clause type/attachment is not fixed until more words appear)
numerical/quantifier openings (Eighteen percent, Around 60 — begin a nominal expression that may attach in different ways until the verb or complementizer appears)
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is standard written English with SVO order and frequent clause embedding via complementizer 'that' and relative pronouns (who/which). Many sentences use sentence-initial adverbial or prepositional phrases and parenthetical appositives, which are part of the surrounding clause rather than true clause boundaries. Coordinating and subordinating conjunctions regularly link full clauses; 'that' often marks embedded clause starts and is a reliable cue to clausehood.
